title: How Scott Colom defied the odds to go from district attorney to Mississippi's Democratic US Senator
description: Scott Colom speaks as he gives an update
body:
Scott Colom speaks as he gives an update on state of Senate race against Cindy Hyde-Smith November 4, 2026 in Jackson, Mississippi. 
                
                    Rogelio V. Solis/Getty Images North America
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Rogelio V. Solis/Getty Images North America
    

   
   JACKSON, Miss. — When Scott Colom, a local district attorney, announced his candidacy late last year, it seemed like a long shot in a ruby red state.   But by October of this year, a month before votes came pouring in for him, he was confident.   "We didn't have hundreds of million dollars to come in to spend – we did it going door to door, festival to festival, earning support," Colom said at a canvassing event on the Mississippi coast. "We're gonna shock a lot of people, but I'm not gonna be shocked. The people of Mississippi are behind this campaign: they understand Mississippi matters."   
   Colom narrowly defeated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, according to a race call by The Associated Press on Wednesday evening, marking one of the most stunning upsets of the midterm elections this year.   Flipping red counties with a focus on affordability    Colom won by less than five thousand votes, with a small fraction of the vote still left to be counted.   While he swept areas of Mississippi that have traditionally leaned left, like Hinds County, home to Jackson, the state capital, he also picked up places that have traditionally voted Republican, like Forrest County, which President Trump won in 2024 with about 58 percent of the vote.   Colom has been the district attorney for the state's 16th judicial district since 2016. That includes his hometown of Columbus, Mississippi, in Lowndes County – an area that's also got a right-leaning voter base.   Colom ran on accessible healthcare, saving rural hospitals and affordability. He said that working in a Republican-majority area informed the need for bipartisanship in tackling those issues.   "I believed that the majority of the Mississippians love our state more than they hate the Democratic party or love the Republican party," Colom said. "They want their kids to have good schools. ... they want to be able to make sure that young people, if they want to stay in Mississippi, can have a job. They want the hospitals to stay open."   
   While Colom isn't surprised that his message resonated this year with voters, he faced obstacles when a federal judicial nomination stalled in the U.S. Senate in 2023, when then-President Joe Biden nominated him for a federal judgeship.   Mississippi's Sen. Roger Wicker, a Republican, indicated he would support his nomination.   The state's Junior Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith blocked him. She cited donations from billionaire philanthropist George Soros around Colom's run for DA, which in 2023, Colom said were to an independent PAC – not his campaign.   She also said he opposed legislation to protect female athletes in a statement provided to the Mississippi Free Press at the time.   In a letter to Hyde-Smith, Colom said he didn't know what she was referring to and noted that he'd signed a statement saying he wouldn't use law enforcement resources to criminalize doctors who offer gender affirming care to transgender youth.   He also stated in the letter that if he was confirmed as a judge, any of his personal views would be irrelevant to his "daily work." And he asked the senator  to reconsider – she didn't.   Three years later, she was defending her seat from him. She was confident, on election night, that she'd beat him, telling her supporters, "I blocked Scott Colom from being a federal judge, and you blocked him from being U.S. senator."   She instead lost and on Wednesday night, she issued a statement conceding the race, saying she respects the decision of Mississippi voters.   A narrow victory that 'made a difference'    Colom recognized that attention from national Democratic leaders, and his party's campaign funds, came late this year, but he noted that it was the attention his campaign received from voters within the state that made the difference.   "They understand the power of their vote in ways that we really haven't seen in a long period of time, because if you look at these margins, certainly everything that everybody did made a difference," Colom told reporters in Jackson just days before the election was called.   
   Being elected as a Democrat is no small feat either. The last time Mississippi sent a Democrat to the Senate was 1982 and an incumbent hasn't been defeated since 1942.   Colom now also holds the distinction of being the state's first Black senator since Reconstruction.    It's something he's proud of – but not the laurels he's resting on.   "My job is to be a senator that makes it easier for the next African American that has the work ethic, the vision, the values, and they want to be United States senator, make it easier for them," Colom said. "I am a person that is continuing to show up in the community and take the tough questions and explain my, you know, live my values. And if I do that, it makes it easier for the next person to be judged by their character and not their skin color."   While his victory is historic, his campaign has also made waves – especially on social media. In an interview with WLOX, Hyde-Smith responded to questions about beef affordability by suggesting folks pick a different protein.   Colom hit back, with a campaign ad, suggesting folks pick another senator instead.   Eventually, the rest of the country started listening. About two weeks before the election, the PAC associated with Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer donated $1.2 million for advertising.   And, several big name Democrats also ended up joining Colom on the campaign trail: former Vice President Kamala Harris, former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, former President Bill Clinton and U.S. Senator Raphael Warnock of Georgia, to name a few.   Colom traveled the whole state – from the coast to the capital, up to the Tennessee border. While in the Mississippi Delta, he said what he wants to do while in the Senate all goes back to his home of Columbus.   "I've always been committed to trying to make my community better, trying to make my city better, trying to make my state better, and that's what running for United States Senate is all about for me," Colom said. "It's a continuation of a service that runs in my family and I was raised [by] my community and my church to give back and that's why I'm doing it in this moment."   
   Tiara Jackson of Mississippi Public Broadcasting contributed to this report.

title: Democrat Scott Colom wins the closest Senate race in the country
description:
Democrat Scott Colom wins the closest Senate race in the country
    
            
                
                Transcript
body:
Democrat Scott Colom wins the closest Senate race in the country
    
            
                
                Transcript
            
        
                Download
                
                
                    
                        
                            
                            Embed
                        
                        
                            <iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/nx-s1-6037840/nx-s1-10001388" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">
                        
                    
                
                
                  
                    
                    Transcript
                  
                
        
    



   Mississippi hadn't elected a Democrat to the U.S. Senate in more than 40 years.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    SCOTT DETROW, HOST:  Mississippi's U.S. Senate race has finally been called. Democratic challenger Scott Colom will be the state's next senator. That is according to a race call by The Associated Press. Colom is the first Democrat elected to the Senate from Mississippi since 1982 and the first African American to represent Mississippi since Reconstruction. Elise Catrion Gregg of the Gulf States Newsroom and Mississippi Public Broadcasting has been following this and joins us now. Hey, Elise.ELISE CATRION GREGG, BYLINE: Hi there.DETROW: I mean, a lot of historic markers there. Walk us through all of this.GREGG: Yeah, absolutely. You know, Colom announced his run in late 2025, and it was seen as just kind of a long shot in a state that has been traditionally a Republican stronghold. And now he's won. When the votes first came in on election night, you know, Cindy Hyde-Smith seemed like she was ahead and, you know, for much of the campaign season, she was, you know, projected to be the winner. Although folks, you know, were aware of Colom's popularity. Here we are now. Latest results show he's roughly 5,000 votes ahead of her.DETROW: Yeah. I mean, a Democratic victory in Mississippi is shocking, even in the context of the wave election that seemed to be building. Mississippi was not on the radar of that many people looking at states that could flip. It's a stunning loss for Republicans. What is the party saying?GREGG: So we haven't gotten any official statements from Republicans in the state or from Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith just yet, although she has called to concede the race. But we do know that before this was all called, the state GOP said that they would be looking into legal options, possible litigation and just really closely monitoring the ballot count. And to be clear, both candidates have had volunteers and lawyers monitoring the count. But what I will say is that we're likely to see some legal action come out of this at some point or another. But, you know, it's very clear, as Scott Colom has said several times during his campaign, especially in recent days, the people of Mississippi have spoken.DETROW: Mississippi doesn't have a recount law, right? It wouldn't be a set process that you know exactly what's going to happen?GREGG: No, it's been interesting to see. There's no recount law, and we don't have runoffs for U.S. Senate race, so plurality wins, and the votes speak for themselves in this case.DETROW: Elise last question - Scott Colom has this historic win, as we mentioned. What do we need to know about Colom?GREGG: Yeah, so since 2016, Colom has been a local district attorney. His platform was on affordability, you know, healthcare accessibility, saving rural hospitals, which is a huge deal here in Mississippi. And he said that his work as a DA in an area that leans right has really informed just his push for bipartisanship and prioritizing issues that matter to Mississippians across the state. When he was a DA, a big priority of his was ensuring that innocent folks weren't being put in prison. In fact, that was part of his platform that helped him win against the previous DA.And he has just had a really robust campaign over the last year or so. He's gone all the way to the coast to the very north part of Mississippi, through the Delta and central Mississippi. He's talked to folks from both parties. I think, notably, when President Trump came to Corinth, Mississippi, for a rally for Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, Colom was in line with folks trying to get in, talking to them about what issues matter to them. He's run a really robust campaign, and I think that's resonated with the voters here in Mississippi.DETROW: That's Elise Catrion Gregg with Mississippi Public Broadcasting and the Gulf States Newsroom. Thanks so much.GREGG: Thank you.(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)

title: At least 23 states considered laws governing ICE and schools this year
description:
Hokyoung Kim for NPR
    

   
   Catch up on what you mi
body:
Hokyoung Kim for NPR
    

   
   Catch up on what you missed with our Education newsletter, sent weekly.      Andrea Garza says it's not unusual or alarming when U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents are spotted near a school in Laredo, Texas, a border town.   In other parts of the country, "seeing the presence of border patrol would be, you know, different, maybe shocking. Just something from another world, right?" she said. "It's something very normal here."   Garza is a school leader with the United Independent School District , which serves Laredo. Federal data shows 94% of her district's community is Hispanic. Garza said some families have been in Laredo for generations, while others came more recently, and the federal government is one of her area's largest employers.   
   She said she knows what she would do if ICE comes knocking: If they don't have a warrant or subpoena, they don't get in.   "We serve 'in loco parentis' for students," she said, meaning "in place of a parent" when the students' rights are challenged.   "It's not interpreted, in the way we see it, as interfering with the law," Garza explained. "It is more just verifying that we are all following the law."   Texas state law prohibits local entities, including campus police, from obstructing federal immigration enforcement. But NPR found no state laws that directly address how much access these officers should have in K-12 public schools.   
   And it's not just Texas. Many states lack clear policies governing what these interactions should look like. Recent federal changes haven't helped.   At the beginning of President Trump's second term, the administration rescinded a policy that protected schools, among other "sensitive" places, from immigration enforcement.   "Criminals will no longer be able to hide in America's schools and churches to avoid arrest," a statement from the U.S. Department of Homeland Security said at the time. "The Trump Administration will not tie the hands of our brave law enforcement, and instead trusts them to use common sense."   
   In some places, school leaders and researchers say Trump's immigration policies have led to enrollment drops.   DHS, which houses ICE, has said that ICE does not raid or target schools.   But reporting from K-12 Dive shows the last academic year still saw several incidents of ICE agents on school grounds. When that happens, education leaders often rely on a patchwork of state and district policies to know what to do.   This year, many state legislatures tried to update those policies.    Loading... 
   An NPR analysis found that, so far this year, at least 23 states have considered new legislative proposals — in some cases multiple proposals — governing federal immigration officers and K-12 public schools.   The vast majority of the state proposals NPR reviewed — 35 out of 40 — sought to limit federal officers' access to K-12 campuses and students; only one proposal — in Mississippi — sought to ensure that schools cooperate with ICE. The rest didn't explicitly limit or increase access or cooperation.   Thomas Saenz is president and general counsel of the Mexican American Legal Defense and Educational Fund, an organization that advocates for Latinos living in the U.S. He said the elimination of the federal sensitive locations policy is likely driving many states to establish their own protections, "belts and suspenders, as they say."   But while lawmakers seem to agree there's a need for clearer policies, in many places, they've struggled to find consensus over what those policies should be. Of the 40 proposals NPR reviewed, only 11 became laws by the beginning of this school year.   From requiring a warrant to requiring cooperation   Minnesota, Arizona, Delaware, Georgia, Maine and Nebraska are among the state legislatures that considered restricting ICE access to schools.   Several of these proposals specified the need for a warrant. Others aimed to restrict what school police and school resource officers, or SROs, can and can't do, including when it comes to immigration-related arrests.    
   On the other side of the spectrum, Mississippi considered and passed a law requiring government entities, including school districts, to cooperate with federal immigration enforcement.   And a few states considered requiring school boards to adopt policies outlining how they would respond to immigration authorities on school property.   At least eight states already had laws governing immigration enforcement and K-12 schools at the start of 2026. A few of those states — including Connecticut, Maryland and Oregon — considered additional legislation this year.   
   Recent state proposals have also aimed to allow public schools to charge tuition for students who aren't U.S. citizens or legal immigrants. Such proposals would challenge the decades-old landmark Supreme Court ruling Plyler v. Doe, which established that all children, regardless of immigration status, have the right to a free K-12 public education.   NPR did not include these proposals in its analysis. According to reporting from Education Week, as of July, at least two states were considering proposals challenging Plyler. Similar efforts failed in at least five other states.   Proposals target sensitive locations and student enrollment   Following the Trump administration's decision to rescind the policy protecting "sensitive" places, some states have been trying to set their own rules around where immigration enforcement can and can't go.   
   A few states — including West Virginia, Hawaii and Kansas — made a push this year to restrict ICE access by designating school campuses as sensitive locations. None of those three states' proposals passed.   Some states already have laws that explicitly ban or restrict these types of sanctuary policies. That didn't stop Missouri from considering a proposal this spring to limit school cooperation with immigration enforcement. An existing state law prohibiting municipalities from adopting sanctuary policies and requiring cooperation calls into question how far such a proposal could go.   Lawmakers in Tennessee considered multiple proposals this year from across the political spectrum, including one to track K-12 students' legal status, which opponents argued was part of an effort to challenge Plyler, and another that would require schools to immediately notify all students, parents and employees if immigration officers were on school grounds.   
   "As legislators, we cannot make informed decisions without data, and right now we simply do not know what the attendance is in our school systems across the state, regarding children who are here illegally," Tennessee Rep. Jason Zachary (R-Knoxville) said in a March hearing, where he spoke in favor of the measure that would have required schools to report students who are undocumented.   The bill did not make it to a final vote.   Meanwhile, another Tennessee proposal this year would have prohibited certain sensitive areas, including schools, from being used as staging areas, processing locations or operational bases for immigration enforcement.   "Everybody deserves to have a great learning environment, and it's hard to teach when you are worried that one of your students is going to be taken," Tennessee Rep. Gabby Salinas (D-Memphis), who sponsored that bill, told NPR. The proposal ultimately failed.   Minnesota principals await legislation   NPR was not able to find a pre-existing state law in Minnesota. But after the immigration crackdown in Minneapolis earlier this year, lawmakers considered at least five different proposals around ICE and schools.   They ranged from stricter warrant requirements to mandating that schools develop procedures for handling requests from law enforcement. None of the five proposals made it to a final vote.   That means school leaders like Principal Kenny Newby are left waiting.   Newby leads Justice Alan Page Elementary School in Maplewood, Minn., just outside the Twin Cities. He said if ICE ever comes to his school, his goal is to be kind, stay calm and be firm.   In the absence of state laws, he said he has his own district's policies to lean on: Staff members are supposed to welcome the ICE officers, start a conversation, ask for required paperwork and notify school-level administrators. Those administrators then reach out to district leaders.   
   If the officers have a warrant, they would be directed to the district office for next steps. Newby stressed: "We would not allow them to have direct contact with students."   Rob Reetz is the principal of Mounds View High School in nearby Arden Hills. He said it would be helpful to have a state law governing how schools are supposed to interact with federal immigration officers; if nothing else, a law like that could simplify interactions between districts.   Right now, Reetz said, if a sports team from his school travels to play against a team from another district and ICE shows up at the game, it's unclear which district's protocols adults should follow.   Still, if ICE does come knocking at his school, Reetz worries they won't necessarily follow rules set by the state or any other entity.   He said he remembers learning in January that federal agents had been spotted at Roosevelt High School in Minneapolis. At the time, MPR News reported that armed U.S. Border Patrol officers came onto school property during dismissal and "began tackling people, handcuffed two staff members and released chemical weapons on bystanders."   "It contributed to this uncertainty about how would our interactions go with immigration enforcement if they were to be on our campus," Reetz said.   Newby echoed these concerns. He said he and his staff would feel more supported if there were "clear expectations on keeping schools a safe place."   Edited by: Nicole CohenAudio produced by: Lauren MigakiResearch by: Natalie Pate, Nicole Cohen, Sarah Knight and Barclay Walsh

title: Senators don't always share bill text online before votes. They should, advocates say
description: Paper copies of amendment votes are set
body:
Paper copies of amendment votes are set on display near the Senate Chamber, on July 1, 2025 on Capitol Hill.
                
                    Tom Brenner For The Washington Post via Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Tom Brenner For The Washington Post via Getty Images
    

   
   If you want to know what bills are under consideration in the Senate, you could follow floor proceedings live on C-SPAN. But, even for parliamentary procedure experts, it can be difficult to understand exactly what's happening.   Among the issues? The text of what the lawmakers are considering isn't always made available for public review before it is voted on. Now, a crosspartisan group of open governance advocates has sent a letter to Senate leadership calling for change. In the letter, first obtained by NPR, they call on the Senate to post bill and amendment text online as soon as it is made available to members.   
   "The public and the press and the whole apparatus that supports the Senate to help understand what legislation is, they don't have access," said Daniel Schuman, an author on the letter and the executive director of the American Governance Institute, a nonpartisan nonprofit dedicated to strengthening the institutions of American democracy.   
   That lack of transparency means "that problems can often sneak through," said Schuman. "At times, this has been a mechanism for the Senate to move legislation to avoid the proper public scrutiny." In 2013, Schuman recalled, Congress quietly repealed provisions of a popular congressional financial disclosure and insider trading law — skirting public scrutiny.   While the Congressional Record — the official record of legislative branch proceedings and debates — does provide information about bill text and proposed amendments, it is not published until after the legislative day concludes. That means when bills or amendments are offered on the same day they are considered, they may not be publicly available until after they are voted on.   "We've been working first to get the Senate to update their own systems internally," said Luke Hogg, a senior fellow at the Foundation for American Innovation, which works to help policymakers become more effective stewards of innovation.    The organization joined AGI on the letter, and as Hogg explained, now that staffers themselves have reliable access to what is being considered, "it should also be given to the American public."   
   In contrast to the Senate, the House of Representatives publishes draft legislative text and proposed amendments online ahead of their consideration, with rare exceptions.   
   The letter argues that the current Senate process creates unequal access to information, where staff and interest groups with connections to Senate offices understand what's being considered, but legislative support agencies like the Congressional Research Service and the Government Accountability Office, as well as the press and public at large are often left in the dark.   "Privileged access to public business that currently is the subject of floor debate should be minimized to the extent possible," the letter says.   The advocates hope to see the Senate enact the public transparency effort in the new Congress in January.    In a statement to NPR, an aide to Sen. Alex Padilla, the California Democrat who is expected to become chairman of the Senate Rules committee, said that the senator is open to input on the transparency measure as well as other ideas to improve the functioning of Congress.   Sen. John Thune, Senate Republican leader, did not respond to a request for comment.

title: A blue wave helped offset for now a falling tally of Black members in the U.S. House
body:
Democratic Reps. Terri Sewell (left) and Shomari Figures of Alabama appear at a voting rights rally in May on the steps of the state's Capitol in Montgomery, Ala.
                
                    Jake Crandall/USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Jake Crandall/USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect
    

   
   A U.S. Supreme Court ruling this year that further weakened the Voting Rights Act raised the possibility of a record drop in Black representation in Congress.   But a Democratic blue wave in the midterm elections helped forestall such a decline for now.   Most notably, Rep. Shomari Figures, a Black Democrat, won reelection despite Alabama's Republican state leaders making his district far more GOP-leaning after the court's decision.   
   Black representation in the U.S. House is still slated to decline next year, according to an NPR analysis. The incoming Congress is set to include 60 Black House members, including nonvoting members, down from 63 in the current House. That's just one away from the record loss of four Black representatives after the 1876 election, around the end of the Reconstruction era.   In addition to the unprecedented mid-decade redistricting fight, the usual churn of politics, including members retiring or running for higher office, contributed to next year's falling tally.   
   But high Black voter turnout, especially in the South, fueled Democratic wins that have offset the upcoming decline in the number of Black members of the House.   Voting rights advocates and redistricting experts warn, however, that the redrawing of district lines in the coming years, including after the 2030 census, continues to pose a threat to Black representation in Congress.   A "Black wave" helped Black Democrats overcome redistricting hurdles in the South   Heading into this year's midterms, Figures faced tough odds of keeping his House seat in Alabama, where voting has been racially polarized between a Republican-supporting white majority and a Democratic-supporting Black minority.   
   Figures joined Congress after the 2024 election as the first Black representative of the state's 2nd Congressional District. As part of a long redistricting battle, a lower federal court had ordered the district to be drawn to include a Black population large enough to have a realistic opportunity of electing their preferred candidate.   For the midterms, though, the Supreme Court's conservative majority allowed Alabama's Republican-controlled legislature to redraw the district. That ruling came weeks after the high court released its landmark decision in Louisiana v. Callais, which weakened the Voting Rights Act's protections against racial discrimination in political mapmaking.   
   The new lines of Alabama's 2nd District, the lower court had previously found, were "tainted by intentional race-based discrimination" and would "afford Black-preferred candidates zero chance of winning there." Based on the redrawn map, Figures appeared to be on track to leave Congress like Rep. Cleo Fields, the Louisiana Democrat who decided not to seek reelection after the Supreme Court's Callais ruling struck down the Black opportunity district Fields represents.   "It took a remarkable level of turnout in order for [Figures] to be able to win," says Cliff Albright, co-founder and executive director of Black Voters Matter. "Some are calling it a blue wave. For us, particularly here in the South, we're calling it a Black wave because what we saw was the Black electorate's been motivated by the attacks on our voting rights, by the gerrymandering that was taking place."   
   New voting maps in Texas and Florida led to the undoing of some Black-represented districts, but Democrats' sweeping victories in other states are helping to counteract those losses.   North Carolina's GOP-controlled legislature redrew the district of Rep. Don Davis, one of the state's three Black representatives, but Davis defended his seat. And two incoming Black House Democrats — Cyril Jefferson and LaKesha Womack — flipped districts long represented by white Republicans.   Democratic socialist Reps.-elect Melat Kiros in Colorado and Donavan McKinney in Michigan are also adding to the tally.   And Democrats are set to take control of statewide offices and legislative chambers in Texas and other places that were long-standing Republican strongholds.   By breaking the GOP trifecta in Georgia, for instance, the blue wave lowered the redistricting threat facing the state's congressional districts represented by Black Democrats. Last week, Georgia's outgoing Republican Gov. Brian Kemp announced he will not call a special session on redistricting before handing the office in January to Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms, who will be the country's first Black woman elected governor.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Rep. Don Davis, a Democrat from North Carolina, speaks at a 2024 campaign event for then-Vice President Kamala Harris in Greenville, N.C.
                
                    David Yeazell/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        David Yeazell/AP
    

   
   Upcoming redistricting could result in fewer Black representatives   But Albright, of Black Voters Matter, sees this year's midterms as unique.   
   "What happens two years from now or four years from now, where it's not the same wave year, where there's not the same economic realities across the country, where you don't necessarily get the same number of white voters that decide, 'Oh, I guess I can vote for this Democrat'?" Albright says. "It's simply not sustainable for Black voters to be carved up and have our voting power that diluted and for it to not have an impact over a more sustained period of time."   And while midterm successes are leading some Democratic politicians to declare a generational shift in U.S. politics, Kareem Crayton, a redistricting expert and vice president of the Brennan Center for Justice's Washington, D.C., office, is taking a more wait-and-see approach.   "This sounds a lot like what people said in 2009 after a lot of massive change happened, including in the South, with the election of Barack Obama. And it wasn't two years later that people sat in a haze, looking at returns that pretty much wiped out many of those changes that favored Democrats, including Black Democrats," Crayton says. "It could be that this is a start of a generational shift, but it might not be. And if you're thinking about how rules ought to be crafted, I think the cautious approach is always the preferable approach in making certain that rights under the worst conditions are protected as opposed to the most rosy scenarios."   
   Crayton says current redistricting rules, shaped by the Supreme Court's decisions in Callais and other cases, set up the potential dismantling of more opportunity districts for Black and other racial minority voters in future years. This past year's redistricting rush was limited partly because the Callais ruling came too late for many states to redraw their maps in time for the midterms.   "I think people who are looking at the recent Supreme Court decision around Callais and how it would be implemented always understood that the greatest reaction to that would not be in 2026, but would be 2028, 2030 and onward," says Dedrick Asante-Muhammad, president of the Joint Center for Political and Economic Studies, which tracks Black representation in Congress.   
   And that reaction is likely to reach beyond Congress, adds Janai Nelson, president and director-counsel of the Legal Defense Fund, which represents a group of Black Louisiana voters in the Callais case.   "When we look at state legislatures, when we look at city councils, when we look at school board maps and we look at any other elected office that relies on districts, those have largely been untouched by Callais up until now," Nelson says. "But as we enter a new state legislative process where these maps may be redrawn, then we might see devastating impact in electability by Black voters across the country and especially in the South."   There's no redistricting, however, for U.S. senators. And on that side of Capitol Hill, Black representation is on the rise. The blue wave of the midterms has lifted the number of Black senators in the new Congress to a historic high of seven. They include Illinois Lt. Gov. Juliana Stratton and fellow Democrat Scott Colom, who is set to become the first Black senator from Mississippi since Reconstruction.   Edited by Benjamin Swasey

schema.headline: A blue wave helped offset for now a falling tally of Black members in the U.S. House
